sections.h2: Who bills and who values property
sections.html:
Two Clayton County offices touch every parcel. The Board of Tax Assessors sets the value. The Tax Commissioner sends the bill, collects the money and divides it among the county, the cities, fire services and the school board. The millage rate is not either office's call: county commissioners set the county rate and each other taxing body sets its own.

Both offices share the Jonesboro government complex at 121 South McDonough Street. The assessors are on the fourth floor of Annex 3, (770) 477-3285. The Tax Commissioner is on the second floor of the same annex, and the property tax line is (770) 477-3311. A value question sent to the commissioner, or a payoff question sent to the assessors, just gets passed along, which costs a seller days.

Value is fixed as of January 1. A house sold in October is still billed to whoever owned it on that January date, so lay the tax bill next to the closing statement and compare.

Clayton sits just south of Atlanta, densely built, with the courthouse in Jonesboro and most of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport inside its lines. The 2020 census counted 297,595 residents, 106,200 households and 114,038 housing units, 6.9% of them vacant. Renters edged out owners, at 50.5% of occupied homes to 49.5%.

That mix means a landlord selling with tenants in place is a common situation here, and the lease is one more thing to settle before a closing date. Ask the Tax Commissioner whether your parcel also carries a city bill, since part of the county sits inside city limits.

The Tax Commissioner describes a yearly rhythm. Assessment notices go out in spring or early summer, the millage rate process runs from about mid July to mid August, and bills follow around mid September. The due date is usually in mid November, with a payment window of 60 days after mail-out. Exact dates move from year to year. The printed bill has them, or call (770) 477-3311.

If your value is under appeal when bills go out, you receive two bills. One covers 85% and falls due with everyone else's. The other covers the remaining 15% and comes due, or comes back as a refund, after the appeal settles. Request both before the house goes on the market.

Georgia adds two rules of its own. Interest starts 60 days after the bill's postmark, and penalties can follow on delinquent balances. A claim for tax assessed in error must begin within three years of payment, and appeal refunds are issued once the final value is set.

You have 45 days from the mailing date shown on the notice, and the appeal must be in writing. Homestead applications and other specialized assessment requests ride on that same date. A late filing forfeits that year's challenge. File with the assessors in Annex 3, or use the county's online appeals site.

After the first review, the notice lists four routes.

Appeal routes after the first review
RouteWhat it can decideCondition printed on the notice
Board of EqualizationValue, uniformity, exemptions or taxabilityOpen to any owner who files in time
Nonbinding arbitrationValue onlyRequires a certified appraisal
Hearing officerValue or uniformityReal property that is not a homestead and is valued above $500,000, plus large personal property accounts
Superior CourtAs agreedOnly by written agreement with the assessors

Within 10 business days of a request, the assessors owe you the records behind your value, so ask early. Bring comparable sales, plus photos of any defects an assessor could not see from the street. The rate itself is off the table, because an appeal reaches value, uniformity and taxability only.

A homestead is the one house you own and live in as your primary residence on January 1, and nobody can hold two. Applications go to the Tax Commissioner. The filing window is January 2 to April 1, and a late application waits for the following year. Once approved, it renews on its own. You only have to report if you stop qualifying.

Clayton voters were also given a local base-year homestead freeze on the county-purposes value for these groups:

  • Residents age 65 or older
  • Disabled former service members
  • Unremarried surviving spouses of peace officers or firefighters killed in the line of duty
  • Residents who are 100 percent disabled

Whether your parcel is covered is a question for the commissioner's office.

A homestead exemption follows the occupant. A buyer files separately after moving in, so the next bill on the house can run higher than yours did.

Unpaid taxes lead to an execution on the property and, eventually, a tax sale. The Tax Commissioner's property portal links to tax sale notices, a bidder pre-registration form, and an excess funds claim form for owners owed money after a sale.

A tax sale transfers a tax deed and not clear title, and Georgia law gives the owner a right to redeem. Lenders will not lend against a house with a lien, and whatever is owed comes off your proceeds at closing. If you are behind, call (770) 477-3311 first and ask what it takes to clear the account by your target closing date.

sections.h2: Selling with a bill outstanding or an appeal pending
sections.html:
Nothing at the county level divides the year between buyer and seller. The contract and the settlement statement, prepared by the closing attorney, do that. Have the closing office request a payoff covering the county bill and any city bill. Before you list:

  • Pull your current bill from the Tax Commissioner's portal and note whether a city bill also applies.
  • Ask whether an appeal is pending, because a pending appeal means a second bill for the remaining 15%.
  • Confirm that any homestead exemption will be removed after the sale.
  • Keep the closing statement. It is your record that the bill was paid.

A sale with tenants or a repair list can still close on a cash timeline, and a cash sale skips the buyer's loan appraisal and underwriting. Compare any written cash offer with what a listing would net after repairs, showings and the wait.

faqs.q: What is the filing deadline for a Clayton County value appeal?
faqs.a: The deadline is 45 days after the mailing date on your notice, and the appeal must be in writing. Take it to the assessors at 121 S. McDonough Street, Annex 3, fourth floor, in Jonesboro, or use the county's online appeals site. A late one leaves the value standing for the year.

faqs.q: Which Clayton County office answers bill questions, and which handles values?
faqs.a: Bills, payments, exemptions and payoffs go to the Tax Commissioner at (770) 477-3311. Values, notices and appeals go to the assessors at (770) 477-3285. The assessors collect nothing, and the commissioner changes no values.

faqs.q: Do I pay anything while a Clayton County appeal is pending?
faqs.a: Yes, most of it. A parcel under appeal receives two bills. The 85% bill is due on the usual date. The other 15% is settled after the decision, and that can mean a small balance or a refund.

faqs.q: Can a Clayton County house with unpaid taxes still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes come out of your proceeds at the closing table, so get a payoff figure for the closing date. A parcel already sold at a tax sale needs one more step, because the tax deed buyer holds an interest until redemption. Start with a call to (770) 477-3311.

faqs.q: Does my homestead exemption pass to the buyer of my Clayton County house?
faqs.a: No. The exemption belongs to the person who lives in the home. A buyer files a new application with the Tax Commissioner, and one filed after April 1 is processed for the following year.
